stem: A 45-year-old man is brought to the hospital by his family due to progressive jaundice and abdominal swelling. He has a 20-year history of consuming approximately 10-12 standard drinks of alcohol daily. He reports a three-week history of anorexia, nausea, and fatigue. On physical examination, he is icteric and has a tender, enlarged liver. Vitals are: temperature 38.1°C, pulse 94/min, blood pressure 110/72 mmHg, respiratory rate 18/min, and oxygen saturation 96% on room air. Laboratory studies reveal a serum bilirubin of 4.2 mg/dL, an AST of 185 IU/L, and an ALT of 72 IU/L. The gamma-glutamyltransferase is significantly elevated. The patient's coagulation profile shows a slightly prolonged prothrombin time.
lead_in: Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: The patient presents with jaundice, tender hepatomegaly, and a history of heavy alcohol use, which is highly suggestive of alcoholic hepatitis. The key diagnostic finding is the AST/ALT ratio; in this patient, the ratio is 2.57 (185/72), which is $\ge 2$. This pattern is characteristic of alcoholic hepatitis, where AST and ALT are modestly elevated (typically < 300-500 IU/L) and AST predominates due to the deficiency of pyridoxal 5'-phosphate, a cofactor for ALT, in alcoholics. Acute viral hepatitis would typically present with much higher transaminase levels (often > 1000 IU/L). Autoimmune hepatitis often shows a different AST/ALT ratio and is associated with other autoimmune markers. Hemochromatosis would typically show a more chronic course and different transaminase patterns. NASH can present similarly but is typically associated with metabolic syndrome and lacks the same dramatic AST/ALT ratio associated with heavy alcohol use.
teaching_point: Alcoholic hepatitis is characterized by jaundice and tender hepatomegaly in patients with heavy alcohol use, with a characteristic AST/ALT ratio $\ge 2$ and transaminases typically below 500 IU/L.

distractor_rationale.A: Presents with much more dramatic transaminase elevations (typically > 1000 IU/L).
distractor_rationale.B: Typically presents with a different transaminase pattern and associated autoantibodies.
distractor_rationale.C: Presents as a chronic process of iron overload, not usually as an acute inflammatory hepatitis.
distractor_rationale.E: Associated with metabolic syndrome and lacks the distinct AST/ALT ratio $\ge 2$ seen in heavy alcohol use.
